name: address-normaliser-rule-recovery
description: Recover ordered rewrite rules from 900 before/after address pairs and implement a Python normaliser that reproduces the retired engine on unseen addresses.
scenario: A municipal government retired its address-normalisation engine. 900 before/after pairs from its log survive in data/addresses.tsv. Your task is to write a Python normaliser (normalise.py) that reproduces the engine's behaviour on new addresses. The engine applied about 25 ordered regex rewrite rules; rule order matters when rules overlap, and some rules fire only rarely. A postal style guide in data/README.md documents the conventions the engine followed.
environment_setup: The Dockerfile is based on python:3.12-slim-bookworm with WORKDIR /app. It copies a stub normalise.py (with --input/--output argparse flags, reads stdin one-address-per-line, writes stdout one-per-line, returns input unchanged), data/addresses.tsv (~900 before\tafter TSV pairs pre-generated from a seeded engine), data/README.md (postal style guide noting uppercase output, period/comma removal, abbreviation expansion, rare rules existence, and near-miss patterns), and tests_public/ (60 simple before\tafter pairs with a run_tests.sh script). No pip packages installed. No network. The generator script used to create the TSV is deleted from the image after build.
instruction_summary: Edit /app/normalise.py to normalise addresses exactly as the retired engine did. Study the training pairs in data/addresses.tsv and the style guide in data/README.md. Your normaliser must read one address per line from stdin (or --input file), write one normalised address per line to stdout (or --output file), and preserve the --input/--output flags. It must reproduce the engine on at least 92% of held-out address pairs. The engine applied about 25 ordered regex rewrite rules; some fire only 2-3 times in the training data, and some patterns that look normalisable are left unchanged.
solution_outline: Write /app/normalise.py implementing all 25 ordered regex rewrites: (1) uppercase, (2) remove periods, (3) remove commas, (4) collapse whitespace, (5) strip, (6) P\s+O\s+BOX → PO BOX, (7) PO BOX # → PO BOX (remove # immediately after PO BOX), (8) PO BOX (\d+) APT → PO BOX \1 #, (8b) PO BOX (\d+) UNIT → PO BOX \1 #, (9) NE→NORTHEAST, (10) NW→NORTHWEST, (11) SE→SOUTHEAST, (12) SW→SOUTHWEST, (13) N→NORTH, (14) S→SOUTH, (15) E→EAST, (16) W→WEST, (17) SUITE→STE, (18) STE→#, (19) APT→#, (20) UNIT→#, (21) RM→ROOM, (22) BLDG→BUILDING, (23) FL→FLOOR, (24-31) ST/AVE/RD/DR/LN/BLVD/PL/CT → full word with lookahead (?=\s*$|\s+#|\s+ROOM|\s+BUILDING|\s+FLOOR)
Ensure rule order: cleanup → PO BOX normalization → compound directions → single directions → SUITE→STE→# chain → APT/UNIT→# → RM/BLDG/FL → street types with lookahead
Final whitespace cleanup after all substitutions
Preserve --input/--output CLI interface and stdin/stdout behavior
test_plan: test_overall_accuracy: Generate 300 held-out pairs from seeds 200-209 using engine.py + generator.py in tests/; run normalise.py on all 'before' addresses via stdin; compare stdout against engine output; require ≥92% exact match (276/300)
test_direction_abbreviation: Filter held-out pairs with single-letter direction prefixes (N/S/E/W); verify all expand to full words (NORTH/SOUTH/EAST/WEST); 15 pairs, 100% required
test_direction_word_preserved: Filter held-out near-miss pairs where NORTH/SOUTH/EAST/WEST appears as a street name; verify the word stays unchanged; 10 pairs, 100% required
test_compound_direction: Filter held-out pairs with NE/NW/SE/SW (including period variants like N.W.); verify correct expansion; 10 pairs, 100% required
test_unit_before_street_type: Filter held-out pairs where street type appears before SUITE/STE/APT; verify street type expands correctly because unit normalization runs first; 12 pairs, ≥90% required
test_period_before_direction: Filter held-out pairs with period-containing direction abbreviations (N.W., S.E. etc.); verify period removal enables direction expansion; 8 pairs, 100% required
test_suite_chain: Filter held-out pairs with SUITE; verify SUITE→# through the STE intermediate (both SUITE and STE become #); 8 pairs, 100% required
test_po_box_apt_unit: Filter held-out pairs with 'PO BOX <num> APT/UNIT'; verify conversion to 'PO BOX <num> #'; 6 pairs, 100% required
test_po_box_hash: Filter held-out pairs with 'PO BOX # <num>'; verify # is removed; 5 pairs, 100% required
test_pobox_no_space: Filter held-out near-miss pairs with 'POBOX' (no space); verify it stays unchanged; 5 pairs, 100% required
test_st_not_at_end: Filter held-out near-miss pairs where ST/AVE appears in non-final position (e.g., ST ANDREWS); verify it stays unchanged; 8 pairs, 100% required
test_stdin_stdout: Pipe 20 held-out addresses through stdin, verify stdout has exactly one normalised address per input line, matching engine output
test_cli_flags: Run normalise.py --input /tmp/test_in.txt --output /tmp/test_out.txt with 10 addresses; verify file I/O works and output matches engine
test_no_data_file_access: Run normalise.py with a restricted file-access wrapper (only /tmp and stdin/stdout allowed); verify it does not open data/addresses.tsv or any other data file at runtime
test_no_obfuscated_lookup: Run normalise.py with import hooks blocking hashlib, codecs, base64, pickle, json.load on non-stdin files; verify it still produces correct output on held-out pairs
test_determinism_selfcheck: Verify generator.py with seed 200 produces identical bytes on two runs; verify seed 201 produces different bytes than seed 200
anti_cheat: The 300 held-out pairs are generated from seeds 200-209, completely different from the training seed 42. A lookup table of the 900 training pairs fails because held-out 'before' addresses never appear in training. The engine is not in the image; the generator script is deleted after building the TSV. No network access prevents calling an external service. Tests disable any import of hashlib/codecs/base64/pickle to prevent obfuscated lookup tables by running normalise.py with import hooks. Tests also verify normalise.py does not read any data files at runtime (restricted file-access wrapper allowing only /tmp and stdin/stdout).
failure_modes:
- Missing a rare rule: the agent doesn't notice PO BOX + APT/UNIT or PO BOX + # patterns among 900 pairs, losing 5-10 held-out pairs
- Wrong rule order: the agent places street type expansion before unit normalization, so AVE before SUITE doesn't expand because the lookahead for # hasn't been set up yet; loses 10-15 pairs
- Over-broad regex: the agent uses \bST\b → STREET without the lookahead, incorrectly expanding ST in 'ST ANDREWS'; loses 8-10 near-miss pairs
- Reverse rule trap: the agent adds NORTH→N thinking the engine contracts direction words, breaking 'NORTH AVE' → 'N AVENUE'; loses 5-8 pairs
- Over-broad PO BOX regex: the agent uses PO\s*BOX (zero-width space) which matches POBOX, breaking the near-miss; loses 3-5 pairs
- Missing compound direction before single: the agent expands N before NE, so 'NE' becomes 'NORTH E' instead of 'NORTHEAST'; loses 5-8 pairs
- Missing SUITE→STE intermediate: the agent directly maps SUITE→# and STE→# but in the wrong order, so SUITE becomes STE (not #) because STE→# already ran; loses 5-8 pairs
shape: rule induction from examples; graded on held-out address pairs
hidden_evaluation: 300 held-out address pairs generated from seeds 200-209 with the same generator that produced the training data (seed 42). The generator creates addresses covering all quirk matrix cells: no-overlap/easy (~90 pairs), 2-rule overlap (~55), 3-rule chain (~30), rare rules (~25), near-miss 1-decoy (~55), near-miss decoy+casing (~45). The engine in tests/ normalises each held-out 'before' address to produce the expected 'after'. The agent's normalise.py is run via subprocess on the 'before' addresses and its stdout is compared line-by-line against the engine output.

ground_truth: The engine is a deterministic list of ~25 ordered regex rewrite rules implemented in tests/engine.py. The generator in tests/generator.py creates address pairs from a seeded random process. For each held-out pair, the test runs the engine on the 'before' address to produce the expected 'after'. The generator is also verified to be deterministic (same seed → same bytes) and different seeds produce different instances.

dial: Share of 300 held-out pairs reproduced exactly; fair range 85-97%, threshold set at 92%. A rule-per-pattern baseline (correct rules but wrong order and no position-dependent lookaheads) scores ~75%. The oracle (exact engine reproduction) scores 100%.
quirk_matrix: {"dimensions": ["rule_overlap: [none, 2_rule, 3_rule_chain]", "rare_rule_freq_in_training: [5_plus, 2_3_instances, 1_instance]", "near_miss: [absent, 1_decoy, decoy_plus_casing]"], "mix": "about 30% easy cells (none/5_plus/absent), the rest medium or hard with at least one non-easy dimension per instance"}
public_tests: 60 visible pairs in tests_public/pairs.tsv covering single-rule cases: simple street type expansion (ST→STREET at end), single direction expansion (N→NORTH), APT→#, PO BOX basic normalization, uppercase/period/comma removal, whitespace collapse. A run_tests.sh script feeds addresses to normalise.py and compares output. These cover about 30% of the engine's behaviour; ordering interactions, rare rules, compound directions, and near-miss patterns appear only in hidden test pairs.
anti_cheese: Output-identity check: the 300 held-out 'before' addresses are generated from seeds 200-209 and never appear in the training data (seed 42). A lookup table of training pairs scores 0% on held-out pairs. Additionally, the tests verify normalise.py processes novel combinations (e.g., a rare rule + a near-miss in the same address) that can only be solved by implementing actual rules. The test runner enforces three runtime gates: (1) a restricted file-access wrapper allowing only /tmp and stdin/stdout, preventing normalise.py from reading data/addresses.tsv or any data file at runtime; (2) import hooks blocking hashlib, codecs, base64, pickle, and json.load on non-stdin files, preventing obfuscated lookup tables; (3) a static scan for suspiciously large string constants or encoded data blocks. A hidden test (test_no_data_file_access and test_no_obfuscated_lookup) exercises all three gates on held-out addresses.
graded_instances: 300 held-out pairs generated from seeds 200-209 using the same generator that produced the training data (seed 42). Each seed produces 30 address pairs with a controlled distribution across quirk matrix cells. The generator is deterministic: same seed → identical byte output (verified by a self-check test). Different seeds produce different address content (also verified). About 30% of held-out pairs are easy (no overlap, common rules, no near-miss); the rest exercise at least one hard dimension. Held-out pairs include combinations of quirk cells not always seen together in training (e.g., rare rule + near-miss in the same address), which a correct rule implementation handles but an overfit or pattern-matching approach may not.
contract: /app/normalise.py reads from stdin, one address per line, writes to stdout, one normalised address per line
If --input FILE is given, read from FILE instead of stdin (same one-per-line format)
If --output FILE is given, write to FILE instead of stdout
Empty input lines produce empty output lines
Exit code 0 on success; non-zero on error
Each non-empty input line produces exactly one output line
The --input and --output CLI flags must be preserved and functional
normalise.py must not read any data file at runtime; only stdin/--input and stdout/--output
normalise.py must not import hashlib, codecs, base64, pickle, or use obfuscated lookup tables

invisible_traps.trap: Implementing \bST\b → STREET without the position-dependent lookahead: on most addresses ST appears at the end so the output matches, but on 'ST ANDREWS RD' the over-broad regex produces 'STREET ANDREWS ROAD' instead of 'ST ANDREWS ROAD'. No runtime error; the output just differs from the engine on specific near-miss patterns.
invisible_traps.stated_in: data/README.md says 'Street type abbreviations are expanded when they appear as the last element of the street part (at the end of the address or immediately before a unit designator)'; training data shows ~10 pairs where ST/AVE in non-final position stays unchanged

invisible_traps.trap: Making the PO BOX regex too broad with zero-or-more spaces (\s*) between PO and BOX: 'POBOX' (no space) gets incorrectly normalized to 'PO BOX'. No runtime error; the output differs only on the 3-5 training near-miss pairs and their held-out counterparts.
invisible_traps.stated_in: data/README.md says 'PO BOX normalization applies to the standard format with spaces'; training data shows 'POBOX 123' → 'POBOX 123' (unchanged)

invisible_traps.trap: Adding a NORTH→N contraction rule after the N→NORTH expansion: on most addresses NORTH never appears as input (only N does), so the rule seems harmless; but on 'NORTH AVE' the contraction fires, producing 'N AVENUE' instead of 'NORTH AVENUE'. No runtime error.
invisible_traps.stated_in: Training data shows 'NORTH AVE' → 'NORTH AVENUE' with NORTH unchanged; README says 'Directional prefixes are expanded' (implying one direction: abbreviations → full words)

invisible_traps.trap: Running STE→# before SUITE→STE: SUITE→STE converts SUITE to STE, but STE→# has already run, so the newly-created STE stays as STE instead of becoming #. On addresses with STE (not SUITE) both orders work; the trap only fires on SUITE addresses. No runtime error; output has 'STE 5' instead of '# 5'.
invisible_traps.stated_in: Training data shows 'SUITE 5' → '# 5' and 'STE 5' → '# 5'; both become #, which requires SUITE→STE before STE→#

quirk_matrix:
  rule overlap (order matters):

reference_access: none

crux: The agent can verify 100% on 900 training pairs but cannot verify held-out accuracy; the gap between training and held-out comes from rare rules (2-3 training instances tested more heavily in held-out), ordering interactions visible only when rules overlap, and near-miss patterns that look normalisable but must not fire.
